It’s a hopeful sign of a revenue stream for AI services at a time when investors are fretting about who’s going to pay for the infrastructure needed to power the technology. Paying out less

 

Companies don’t always cut their dividends for scary reasons. But they often do.

 

As the third quarter wraps up, one indicator shows dividend cuts are on the rise. Among thousands of public companies tracked globally by TMX Wall Street Horizon, about 19% of dividend-payout announcements during the quarter have been for reductions, rather than for increases or no change.

 

That would be the highest proportion since the second quarter of 2020 when the Covid-19 pandemic slammed into the global economy.

 

The absolute numbers aren’t huge. In the U.S., 11 companies tracked by TMX Wall Street Horizon have announced continuing but lower dividends during the third quarter. 

 

Two were food sellers, Conagra and Campbell’s. Many staples companies have been squeezed between rising costs and pricing pressures.

 

Idiosyncratic stories can be told about any individual dividend cutters. But for broader market investors, the overall trend matters, too. With Treasury yields on the rise, stocks may be increasingly vulnerable to bonds stealing their thunder, particularly among investors who care about actual cash payouts.

 

Right now, 10-year Treasury Inflation-Protected Securities’s real yield (around 2.6%) is well above the S&P 500’s forward dividend yield (about 1.4%, according to FactSet). Before 2023, S&P 500’s dividend yield had exceeded that TIPS yield for many years.

 

Of course, companies don’t exclusively cut dividends for bad reasons. Sometimes it is related to a merger. A management team may also choose to strategically retain earnings to invest in its business. That shift doesn’t alter the company’s overall earnings “yield,” or the inverse of its price-to-earnings ratio. This often gets compared with bonds, too.

 

Such reallocations might seem especially likely these days with companies facing an enormous need to spend on AI, both for offensive and defensive reasons.

 

Still, it would be unusual to see a rash of dividend cuts purely for strategic needs. A review by McKinsey examined the actions of some 1,200 large public companies with multiyear stable dividends from 1995 to 2021. It found that “virtually no company” in their sample “made a significant dividend cut out of choice rather than need, let alone to fund a bold investment for future growth.”

 

Instead, McKinsey’s review found the most common reasons for dividend cuts were the less-flattering ones. The majority were during crisis times, in 2008 and 2020. The other big driver was decreasing profitability.

 

Another course is for companies to reduce other forms of capital returns to shareholders—stock buybacks. TMX Wall Street Horizon also found that the number of buyback announcements in the quarter was on track to possibly be the lowest in a decade. Even some tech giants have cut back on buybacks.

 

But unless this time really is different, a surge in dividend cuts would tell a much more concerning story.

↗️ Shopify: The online shopping platform is teaming up with Meta, with plans to allow its Muse AI agent to complete purchases on behalf of users with the e-commerce platform’s roster of stores. Shares advanced premarket.
